title: precision-parity-sensitivity-spreadsheet-notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note and lightweight calculator layout for comparing precision choices (4-bit, INT8, FP8, baseline FP16/BF16) across three axes: cost, quality (eval delta), and latency/throughput. The goal is to produce a reproducible spreadsheet that teams can use to pick a quantization profile for a workload and to define rollout gates for production.

Context / motivation:
- We regularly see model-ops tradeoffs: quant gives cost/throughput wins but can introduce small quality regressions and latency variability.
- Need a simple, explainable decision surface so SREs, platform, and product engineers can agree on thresholds and rollout steps.
- This document describes the spreadsheet layout, key formulas, recommended heuristics, and a suggested A/B/canary plan.

Assumptions used in examples below (adjust per workload):
- Baseline model: 7B open-model, FP16 run on instance type A (price assumed $3.00 / GPU-hour).
- Typical request: sequence length = 128 tokens. Average generation length = 50 tokens.
- Baseline throughput (FP16): 100 tokens/second per GPU (rough example). Baseline p95 latency for a 50-token generation ~ 0.5s.
- INT8 throughput improvement: +40% (1.4x). FP8 improvement: +25% (1.25x). 4-bit improvement: +70% (1.7x) but with higher risk of quality drop. These are placeholders—measure for each model.

Key metrics definitions (spreadsheet columns):
- scenario_id: short name for scenario (e.g., high-q-low-cost, bursty-latency-sensitive)
- model_variant: model name + checkpoint + compile flags
- precision: {FP16,BF16,FP8,INT8,4-bit}
- instance_type: GPU SKU / price per GPU-hour
- tokens_per_second: measured throughput in tokens/sec for the scenario
- costs_per_gpu_hour: price string (e.g., $3.00)
- cost_per_1M_tokens = (costs_per_gpu_hour / (tokens_per_second * 3600)) * 1e6
- avg_latency_ms: measured average end-to-end latency for the request shape (ms)
- p95_latency_ms: measured p95 latency (ms)
- quality_metric: eval score used (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE/ExactMatch/WinRate/LLR) and the numeric value
- quality_delta_pct = 100 * (quality_variant - quality_baseline) / quality_baseline (positive = improvement)
- notes: short text

Calculator formulas (copy into spreadsheet):
- tokens_per_hour = tokens_per_second * 3600
- cost_per_token = costs_per_gpu_hour / tokens_per_hour
- cost_per_1M_tokens = cost_per_token * 1e6
- relative_throughput = tokens_per_second_variant / tokens_per_second_baseline
- effective_latency_change_pct = 100 * (p95_latency_variant - p95_latency_baseline) / p95_latency_baseline

Worked example row (numbers illustrative):
- scenario_id: conversational-default
- model_variant: model-x-v2
- precision: FP16 (baseline)
- instance_type: A100-40GB ($3.00/hr)
- tokens_per_second: 100
- cost_per_1M_tokens: (3 / (100*3600)) * 1e6 = $8.33
- p95_latency_ms: 500
- quality_metric: 87.2 (WinRate)
- quality_delta_pct: 0
- notes: baseline

Variant: INT8
- tokens_per_second: 140 (1.4x)
- cost_per_1M_tokens: (3 / (140*3600)) * 1e6 = $5.95
- p95_latency_ms: 420 (improved)
- quality_metric: 86.9
- quality_delta_pct: -0.34%
- notes: small drop in win-rate, strong cost win

Variant: 4-bit
- tokens_per_second: 170
- cost_per_1M_tokens: (3 / (170*3600)) * 1e6 = $4.90
- p95_latency_ms: 380
- quality_metric: 85.6
- quality_delta_pct: -1.84%
- notes: larger quality regression; candidate for non-critical or fallback route only.

Decision heuristics (suggested):
- If quality_delta_pct <= -0.5% and cost_savings >= 25% -> consider INT8 with canary and close monitoring (depends on metric importance).
- If quality_delta_pct <= -1% and cost_savings >= 40% -> only for non-core user traffic or background tasks; require human review and extended eval set.
- For lat. sensitive services (p95 target < 300ms): prefer variants where p95_latency improves or stays within +10% of baseline.
- If metric is user-perceived (CTR, win-rate), use stricter gates (max -0.2% before ramp). For synthetic LLM score metrics (LLR) gates can be relaxed (~0.5%).

Rollout checklist / gating strategy:
1) Offline: run the eval harness over production prompt set (N >= 5k diverse prompts) and compute quality_delta_pct per segment.
2) Perf bench: measure tokens/sec and p95 at target sequence distributions. Calibrate for batching levels you expect in production.
3) Shadow traffic: route 100% of requests to baseline but collect predictions from variant (no user visible). Compare latencies and outputs.
4) Canary 1% traffic: route 1% of live traffic to variant with logging and alerting. Roll for 24-72 hours.
5) Canary 10%: if canary 1% shows stable metrics and no alerts, expand to 10% for 1–2 weeks.
6) Ramp to target: use linear ramping with automated rollback triggers on quality or latency regressions beyond thresholds.

Notebook / spreadsheet layout recommendation (one sheet per model-family):
- Sheet columns (A..M): scenario_id, model_variant, precision, instance_type, tokens_per_second, tokens_per_request, cost_per_1M_tokens, avg_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, quality_metric, quality_delta_pct, notes, decision_recommendation
- Additional supporting sheets: raw_eval_scores, latency_bench_raw, instance_pricing_reference, rollout_log

Sensitivity experiments to include (rows/sections):
- Sequence length sensitivity (8, 32, 128, 512) — quantization can interact with prompt length due to kv-cache memory changes and kernel choices.
- Batch size sensitivity (1, 2, 8, 32) — some quantized kernels prefer smaller/larger batches; report latency and throughput jointly.
- Temperature / sampling mode — sampling variability may amplify perceived quality differences; use same RNG seeds for A/B micro-tests where possible.
- Prompt-type segmentation: system prompts, single-turn, multi-turn, code generation, instruction-following; compute per-segment deltas.

Notes on measurement pitfalls and gotchas:
- Don’t compare token/sec across two different sequence length distributions — always normalize to a fixed request profile or use cost_per_1M_tokens.
- GPU spot pricing can make hourly costs volatile; store both on-demand and spot prices in the instance_pricing_reference sheet.
- Some compiler/engine optimizations (kernel selection) can change latency shape (lower p50 but worse p95); always report p95.
- Quality regressions can be non-uniform across user segments; look for outlier prompt categories.

Operational recommendations (runtime knobs):
- Per-route precision routing: allow a route to specify precision whitelist and fallback policy (e.g., prefer INT8, fallback to FP16 if quality check fails).
- Dynamic precision per request: use a cheap heuristic classifier to send high-risk prompts to baseline precision.
- Hybrid approach: use INT8 for tokens after the first N tokens in long generations (prefix-preserving quantization).

Next steps / action items:
- Convert this sheet layout into a shared Google Sheet template under product/optimize and add example rows for 3 model families. (owner: Sara Patel).
- Engineering to run perf bench for model-x-v2, model-y-13b on INT8/FP8/4-bit and populate raw_bench sheet (owner: Marcus Lee).
- Research to produce per-layer sensitivity map for 4-bit fallback heuristics (owner: Elena Garcia).

Open questions / discussion points for working session:
- What is the right quality gate for customer-facing conversational threads? (-0.2% vs -0.5%)
- Should cost savings threshold be relative to committed pricing for Dedicated customers? (committed capacity makes per-GPU cost different)
- Can we capture user-level signals fast enough to auto-roll back on small quality regressions?

Appendix: quick formula references you can paste into spreadsheet cells:
- = (COST_PER_GPU_HOUR / (TOKENS_PER_SECOND * 3600)) * 1000000  -> cost per 1M tokens
- = 100 * (QUALITY_VARIANT - QUALITY_BASE) / QUALITY_BASE  -> quality delta pct
- = TOKENS_PER_SECOND_VARIANT / TOKENS_PER_SECOND_BASE  -> throughput ratio

This doc is intentionally conversational and contains placeholders. Replace the example numbers with measurements from our bench harness and record the bench commit hash in the rollout_log sheet.

End of note.
